DECLARATION OF JACK HENNINGFIELD, PHD I, Jack Henningfield, declare as follows: 1. My name is Jack Henningfield. I have personal knowledge about the facts set forth in this declaration. 2. A copy of my curriculum vitae is attached as Exhibit A. The information in my CV is true and correct. It includes a more detailed description of my education, training, appointments, publications, and awards. I have a PhD in experimental psychology with a pharmacology supporting program from the University of Minnesota; postdoctoral training in psychopharmacology at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and the University of Minnesota Medical School Department of Psychiatry; and a BA in psychology from the University of Minnesota. 3. Currently, I am Vice President for Research, Health Policy and Abuse Liability at Pinney Associates, and Adjunct Professor of Behavioral Biology, Part-time Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Behavioral Biology Division. I am a consultant to the American Kratom Association and previously provided pro bono support to the same group in its efforts to prevent the Drug Enforcement Administration (“DEA”) from banning kratom. Kratom (Mitragyna speciosa) is a tropical tree native to Southeast Asia, particularly Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Papua New Guinea. Its leaves contain compounds that can have psychoactive (mind-altering) effects. 14. Kratom can act as a stimulant or sedative depending on dosage. Low doses may produce increased energy, alertness, and sociability. Higher doses may produce pain relief, relaxation, and euphoria. Kratom is typically consumed as crushed leaves, powder, capsules, liquids, or brewed into tea. Kratom was traditionally used in Southeast Asia for fatigue and to improve stamina (by laborers), pain relief, and for opium withdrawal. In the U.S. and elsewhere, kratom is used (often self-prescribed) for chronic pain, anxiety or depression, and opioid withdrawal or substitution. 15. Kratom does not produce opioid-like respiratory depressant effects, nor carry opioid-like risks of death. These factual statements have been evaluated and verified as true by the DEA, the U.S. Assistant Secretary of Health, and the World Health Organization’s Expert Committee on Drug Dependence, which conducted an initial review to determine if kratom warranted a full review as a potential path to international scheduling and determined that the evidence did not warrant such. 16. Kratom is not an opioid or narcotic by nature of its botanical origin, by chemical structure, its known overall pharmacology, or by having the high abuse potential and national drug threat assessment necessary to meet statutory requirements for U.S. Controlled Substances Act (“CSA”) Scheduling or requirements for inclusion in the United Nations International Drug Control Treaties. 17. Kratom does not carry a high risk of death. To the contrary, the risk of death by kratom alone is described by FDA and NIDA as rare and generally involving other drugs. There is no consensus on the basis by which kratom might cause death, in contrast to most substances that contribute to overdose deaths (e.g., respiratory depression by opioids and sedatives, cardiovascular incidents by stimulants). While there are rare reports of kratom-caused deaths, virtually all of them appear to be polydrug overdoses. If a kratom user died from a kratom overdose 5

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-33 Filed 03/02/26 Page 7 of 14 or kratom caused cardiac event, it would be a very rare and idiosyncratic event given how few deaths are reported among 10 to 20 million kratom users. There are no reported deaths in Southeast Asia. A recent FDA statement also states that while “in rare cases,” it has been reported that “deaths have been associated with kratom use,” “in these cases, kratom was usually used in combination with other drugs, and the contribution of kratom in the deaths is unclear.” Ex. 20. 18. Kratom is an overall public health asset that is regularly used by millions of people as a harm reduction approach to reduce or eliminate the use of opioids, sedatives, stimulants, and alcohol. Most people use kratom for health and well-being, including as a supplement to, or replacement for, caffeinated beverages and to self-manage depression, anxiety, pain, opioid and other drug withdrawal. 19. The experience of Americans is the same as has been well-established over decades, if not centuries, in Southeast Asia, where there have been no reported deaths. This same product was brought to the United States, where kratom is consumed through tea, decoctions, and other approaches. If a kratom product is composed of natural products, meaning that it is not boosted artificially in alkaloids, there is no FDA or legal requirement to submit a new dietary ingredient application to sell kratom and as summarized by the Department of Justice, DEA, kratom sales are legal in the US except in jurisdictions where they are specially banned. Kratom was not banned for legal sale in the state of Louisiana prior to 2025. 20. The vast majority of the evidence upon which I base my opinions was generated by independent researchers primarily supported by the National Institutes of Health (“NIH”) and NIDA. Such studies have been published at an increasing rate year by year over the past decade in leading biomedical research institutions, including Johns Hopkins, the University of Florida, the NIDA intramural program itself, and many others. A small fraction (likely a few percent) of such publications were supported by commercial companies. 21. As a result of kratom’s known benefits to the public and the apparently low if not non-existent risk of kratom use, kratom is a legally marketed product in 43 states, and it is legal for people in those states to possess and consume kratom. Several of the states that placed kratom 6

Kratom is legally sold in the United States, with the exception of six states and some other jurisdictions. On August 31, 2016, the DEA announced its intent to temporarily add kratom to Schedule I of the CSA “to avoid an imminent hazard to the public safety.”1 In response, U.S. citizens submitted numerous formal comments providing compelling evidence and testimony that kratom is not harmful, but rather critical to healing, managing pain, and combating opiate and alcohol addiction.2 These comments explained that kratom is safer than prescription opioids and that, compared to opioids, deaths attributable to kratom overdose are essentially non-existent. 23. U.S. Representatives Mark Pocan (D-WI) and Matt Salmon (R-AZ) sent a letter to the DEA and the Office of Management and Budget—a letter that received bipartisan support and was signed by 50 members of Congress—against the ban. The letter noted that kratom is an internationally consumed herb and condemned the proposed ban as “hasty” because of known beneficial effects of kratom. The letter said that a ban would adversely affect consumer access to kratom’s known benefits and undermine innovative products that could be used to treat individuals suffering from addiction. 24. Since Dr. Giroir’s kratom scheduling rescission letter, there have been several hundred new published research reports that further strengthen the case for kratom not being appropriate for scheduling. The DEA has not taken further action with respect to kratom. 32. In December 2021, the Expert Committee on Drug Dependence (“ECDD”) at the World Health Organization, comprised of 12 international experts on substance safety and addiction, unanimously concluded that there was insufficient evidence to recommend a critical international scheduling review of kratom. “People report using kratom to self-medicate a variety of disorders and conditions, including pain, opioid withdrawal, opioid use disorder, anxiety and depression,” the ECDD said in its report. “Kratom is being used as a part of traditional medicine in some countries.” “The Committee considered information regarding the traditional use and investigation into possible medical applications of kratom” and “concluded that there is insufficient evidence to recommend a critical review of kratom.”10 33. The FDA has not begun to promulgate or issue a proposed or final rule specific to the regulation of kratom and has only recently begun to conduct formal scientific studies of kratom. In January 2024, the FDA posted a new grant opportunity to fund the first clinical trial “to characterize the abuse potential and subjective effects of botanical Kratom.”11 34. Acceptance by the FDA of a New Dietary Ingredient Notification (“NDIN”) is not a requirement for legal sale of kratom. The FDA only requires an NDIN for a drug product, a dietary supplement, or a food additive in conventional food. Because kratom is legally marketed as a food, the NDIN is optional. 38. I agree with the July 29 DHHS and FDA conclusions as discussed in detail in my 8- factor analysis of 7-OH which I submitted to DEA, FDA, and NIDA on September 29, 2025.
